aspects.says: Check-then-act on a shared map is broken without computeIfAbsent or a lock.
aspects.reason: atomicity violations such as check-then-act are the subject of lesson 5.3.2, which practises them; this page only names the pitfall

aspects.says: Final fields carry their own guarantee: once the constructor finishes, every thread sees their values, provided this did not escape.
Program order, a volatile write read later, thread start and thread join create happens-before edges, and the order is transitive.
An unlock gives an edge only to later locks of the same monitor; different monitors give no visibility.
Immutable objects are thread-safe because their state is set once, through final fields, and never changes.
Main and working memory are a mental model; the JMM itself is defined by actions, program order, synchronization order and happens-before.
Reads and writes of a plain long or double are not guaranteed atomic.
aspects.reason: asked by the quiz on 5.1.2, whose Q5 answer treats it in full; a torn read cannot be produced on a 64-bit JVM, so no test could show it

aspects.says: An object is published safely through a volatile field, a final field, a lock or a static initializer, and a plain field can expose it half built.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: A plain flag set by one thread may never be seen by another thread spinning on it, and volatile fixes that.
aspects.reason: practised on 5.1.4 by 'A stop flag the JIT cannot hoist', the lesson that explains why the loop never sees the write

aspects.says: JMM bugs depend on timing and hardware, so passing unit tests prove little and stress tools such as jcstress are needed.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: advice about testing practice that no graded test can check; the 5.1.4 quiz asks the related point that runs on x86 hide reordering bugs

aspects.says: Atomicity, visibility and ordering are separate concerns that need different tools: atomics, volatile, or a lock.
Virtual threads follow the same JMM rules as platform threads.
aspects.reason: named here as a Java 21 feature only; virtual threads are the subject of the course's module 26
